articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission has made a recommendation to City Council to develop a plan for affordable housing using the city’s share of Alameda County Measure A-1 funds. The City of Piedmont was notified four years ago, in 2017, that its share of the county funds would be in excess of $2,000,000. The city’s Planning Commission and its Ad-Hoc Subcommittee on Measure A-1 has recommended that the city launch a low-interest loan program for the construction of rent-restricted Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), commonly known as granny flats. The low-interest loan program could be used towards a traditional multi-family development as the loans are repaid, according to the Committee’s recommendation. Traditional multi-family developments were not recommended at this time due to zoning revisions, which would not be possible within the constraints of the County’s timeline for receipt of Measure A-1 funds. “Unlike the other jurisdictions in Alameda County, Piedmont does not have properties that are readily available for multi-family development,” said Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson. “They are generally too small in size or are occupied by an ongoing use that is not for multi-family. To transition city-owned land for multi-family development would require general plan amendments and revisions to zoning regulations. These are processes that take a good deal of community engagement and time, time that the county’s timeline does not provide.” Voters adopted Measure A-1 in 2016, the Alameda County Affordable Housing Bond, a $580 million property tax revenue bond. The County Board of Supervisors established guidelines for the use of that funding in 2017, and directed that funds be used to create new and affordable housing. Piedmont received a base allocation of $2.2 million in the form of a low interest loan at 3%. articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont Firefighters Association (PFFA) expressed its stance of opposition to a vaccine mandate in the lead up to the city council meeting on September 7. I would like to offer further explanation on the PFFA stance. Along with the California Professional Firefighters (CPF) and International Association of Firefighters (IAFF), the PFFA’s opposition is not a rebuking of science, an advocate of conspiracy theory or dismissal of the importance of vaccines, but rather a demonstration of the relationship between labor and management. The PFFA is clear that the legal authority rests with the city to enact and enforce a mandate, but also implores the city administration to negotiate the details and impacts of such a mandate. Any workplace mandate has the potential to greatly affect workers. It is the union’s responsibility to be sure that those effects are not detrimental or unfair. As of the September 7 meeting and given the information available, union leadership was not prepared to offer support of a directive that was not fully developed into policy. The goals of the City and the PFFA with regard to addressing Covid are not at odds. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) has raised working capital to upgrade and rebuild K-12 school buildings with 30-year bond issuances. To repay bond investors the working capital (principal) plus interest, property owners in Piedmont are being charged a debt service line item on their property taxes. Lately, the school district has been exclusively issuing competitively priced current interest bonds to ensure the lowest total repayment cost to the taxpayer and funding new construction with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP). Last year voters passed Measure UU which authorizes the City of Piedmont to issue bonds for a brand new aquatic facility. I endorsed Measure UU and asked to be on its bond oversight committee. Per conversations with the city finance director, I was told this committee will not be formed in time for public oversight of the structure of the new city bond. This structure will be somewhat different than that used by the school district. Financial advisors to the city, including Hilltop Securities and the city’s own Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee recommend utilizing a modified current interest bond, called a Premium Bond. In premium bonds, the “true principal” lent to a municipality is divided into two pieces: 1) a par value of the bond that is charged an interest rate, and 2) a premium that is not charged any interest rate. Both pieces can be used as working capital, however bond legal advisors do not consider the premium as being part of the principal being lent. Financial advisors recommend looking at the “true interest rate” based on the “true principal”. Why go through the trouble of splitting up the working capital in this fashion? The fine print of Measure UU revealed that the aquatic facility was expected to cost $23 million. Issuing a Premium Bond allows the city to raise $23 million in total proceeds (working capital) from a bond underwriter while only disclosing $19.5 million in “principal” to the public. To enhance the aquatic center, the city Finance Director is preparing to raise as much working capital as the city can while charging annual property taxes of $26.20 per $100,000 in assessed valuation. Interest rates have fallen since the election and the city may raise more than $25 million. Did the public actually consent to service the repayment of as much debt as the city can raise while charging annual taxes at the maximum disclosed to the public? In reading interviews and watching public debates with Measure UU proponents Betsy Andersen and Bob McBain, I was led to believe – as I believe others were – that we were voting on a maximum debt of $19.5 million.
articles.title: Public consent for Premium Bonds?

By Hari Titan, Ph.D. Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) has raised working capital to upgrade and rebuild K-12 school buildings with 30-year bond issuances. To repay bond investors the working capital (principal) plus interest, property owners in Piedmont are being charged a debt service line item on their property taxes. Lately, the school district has been exclusively issuing competitively priced current interest bonds to ensure the lowest total repayment cost to the taxpayer and funding new construction with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP). Last year voters passed Measure UU which authorizes the City of Piedmont to issue bonds for a brand new aquatic facility. I endorsed Measure UU and asked to be on its bond oversight committee. Per conversations with the city finance director, I was told this committee will not be formed in time for public oversight of the structure of the new city bond. This structure will be somewhat different than that used by the school district. Financial advisors to the city, including Hilltop Securities and the city’s own Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee recommend utilizing a modified current interest bond, called a Premium Bond. In premium bonds, the “true principal” lent to a municipality is divided into two pieces: 1) a par value of the bond that is charged an interest rate, and 2) a premium that is not charged any interest rate. Both pieces can be used as working capital, however bond legal advisors do not consider the premium as being part of the principal being lent. Financial advisors recommend looking at the “true interest rate” based on the “true principal”. Why go through the trouble of splitting up the working capital in this fashion? The fine print of Measure UU revealed that the aquatic facility was expected to cost $23 million. Issuing a Premium Bond allows the city to raise $23 million in total proceeds (working capital) from a bond underwriter while only disclosing $19.5 million in “principal” to the public. To enhance the aquatic center, the city Finance Director is preparing to raise as much working capital as the city can while charging annual property taxes of $26.20 per $100,000 in assessed valuation. Interest rates have fallen since the election and the city may raise more than $25 million. Did the public actually consent to service the repayment of as much debt as the city can raise while charging annual taxes at the maximum disclosed to the public? In reading interviews and watching public debates with Measure UU proponents Betsy Andersen and Bob McBain, I was led to believe – as I believe others were – that we were voting on a maximum debt of $19.5 million. articles.text: Piedmont robotics kicks off this fall with the largest number of teams and students ever, with 50 teams and more than 340 students ranging from kindergarten to 12th grade. Organized by Piedmont Makers, the teams span all four divisions of FIRST Robotics including: 20 teams of K-3rd graders, 20 teams of 4th-7th graders, nine teams of 7th-12th graders, and an elite FIRST Robotics Competition high school team. Piedmont’s FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team, the Highlanders, now has 25 members and has started moving into its new home, the Engineering Lab in the new high school STEAM building. The team has begun training its recruits in software, computer aided design (CAD), precision tool skills and digital fabrication using a 3D printer, laser cutter and CNC router. The preparation will be needed in January, when details of the new game, Rapid React, are released. Helen Potter is Vice President of Piedmont’s FIRST Robotics Competition, and her husband John Lambert is the VP of the Engineering Lab. In a joint statement they expressed what the growth of Makers means to their family and the community. “This is our 6th season of our kids participating in the Piedmont Makers FIRST Robotics teams. We have seen the program grow as our kids have grown up. -Helen Potter Piedmont Makers Fourth graders from the Robotic Rulers, a First Lego League team, assemble a Drive Base and build models for the First Lego League Challenge Robot Game. It’s not surprising this program is so successful. Kids are learning engineering, business and leadership skills but most importantly they are having fun, learning to work together and getting involved in their communities. There is no other robotics league this size in Northern California. It’s a huge asset to our community,” Potter said. Nine teams of 7th-9th graders will compete in the First The Cookoo Carrots robotics team works on an obstacle course. Tech Challenge competition with teams ranging from five to 15 students. These teams are challenged to design, build, program, and operate their robot to compete in head-to-head challenges. The challenges consist of both autonomous (self-driving) and driver-controlled periods. The 4th-7th grade teams will compete in the first ever Piedmont City championship in November before participating in regional qualification tournaments in January. A total of 20 teams of Piedmont K-3rd graders will be competing in the FIRST LEGO League Explore program. This year’s theme is Cargo Connect. Teams will think of ideas for different ways to transport cargo, and will create a team model showing how cargo is sorted and transported to its destinations. Piedmont Makers is a local non-profit dedicated to support and inspire STEAM education in Piedmont and beyond. To learn more about Piedmont Makers and its robotics program, visit www.piedmontmakers.org/ robotics.

articles.text: It’s the time of year when pumpkin spice and purple both make their appearance. Everyone noticed more than a little bit of purple around town yesterday, Tuesday, September 21, the official launch day of the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign. Balloons and signs greeted families as they dropped off their children at school in the morning, and many students and parents wore purple during the day to show support for the Giving Campaign, Piedmont School District’s largest annual fundraiser. This year’s theme, “Forward Together” perfectly encapsulates the community’s commitment to ensuring an excellent education for all students. The Giving Campaign’s traditional kick-off popsicle party returned after school on Tuesday, as excited students and their families gathered to enjoy a popsicle party in front of the Exedra, with popsicles donated by Mulberry’s Market. While the popsicle parties, community events, and outreach may all look easy, the magic doesn’t just happen. The Giving Campaign is powered by both an amazing staff at PEF and an highly dedicated committee of volunteers. Working for months, they put up banners and balloons at the schools, and conduct community outreach writing letters and making phone calls. This year’s committee, one of the largest yet, has more than 60 parents representing all Piedmont schools. Lola Ruthven (left) enjoys a popsicle as Lucy Graham goes back for seconds from the baskets of popsicles being handed out by Piedmont Education Foundations’ Heather Miel and Giving Campaign Co-Chair Colleen Allan.

articles.text: Piedmont School District sent a request to parents on August 24 requesting the COVID-19 vaccination status of all 6th-12th graders. The district currently has 1,222 students enrolled who are 12 years old or older and are eligible to receive the Covid vaccine. As of September 21, after two weeks of the survey, 928 students (75.9%) have declared that they have been fully vaccinated for two weeks. A total of 204 students (16.7%) have not yet responded to the survey, and 82 students (7.4%) stated they have not been fully vaccinated. The survey offered two options: • Yes, fully vaccinated and two weeks post • No, not fully vaccinated No option for partial vaccination or intent to get vaccinated was listed on the survey. The survey asked parents to upload an image of vaccination card or state’s QR code. “The data we’ve received has saved many hours of health staff time.” said Stephanie Griffin, District Director of Technology, at the September 14 School Board meeting. In the event of a positive Covid case at school, the district can now act more swiftly. “If you have an exposure at school and are vaccinated and were in a mask, nowadays, you can continue to come to school and just monitor for symptoms. Last year, [when] anyone was exposed, we would be asking them to quarantine for 11-14 days,” said Griffin. While the survey was not mandatory, the 83% response rate from parents in four weeks has been lauded by the district. On August 23 the Pfizer vaccine was upgraded from emergency approval to full FDA approval for those age 16 and up. Emergency approval of the Pfizer vaccine was granted on May 10, 2021 to allow for those 12-15 to receive the vaccine. The survey will be resent monthly to families who have not responded, newly eligible students, and those who stated they were not vaccinated.

articles.text: Starting strong requires establishing successful habits early. But staying means remembering that hard work, not natural gifts are what leads to success. We all know that the school year starts off slowly, but that doesn’t mean that student should also. articles.text: As the seasons go by and summer turns into fall, holidays start popping up all over the calendar. I get so excited when fall and winter come around because the temperature drops, everything turns a wonderful shade of orange, red, and yellow, you get to start wearing warmer clothes. Halloween decorations start appearing, and a bit later we see Christmas decorations. My birthday is in the winter, so it’s another reason why I love the colder months. When people ask the generic question, “What is your favorite season?” I always respond with winter. If you’re cold, you can put on a sweater, get a comfy blanket, and sip a nice mug of tea or hot chocolate. In the summer months you can do nothing but suffer. You just follow a fan around, drink water every 30 seconds so as not to overheat, and learn to tolerate the humidity. When the temperatures start to fall, so do the painted leaves. Each leaf has its own design and colors. When they gracefully float down to the ground they make it look like a fairyland. Then some short months later the snow falls (in regions that have snow), creating a serene, snowglobe like world. When I walk to school I can hear the crunch of leaves under my feet, something that gives me a good feeling about the day. Come on, who doesn’t like hearing the crunch of leaves under your feet? Coming up soon is good ol’ All Hallows Eve. I haven’t been more excited to dress up in a cheap costume and walk around the town with my friends in a long time. Granted, I don’t think trick or treating has made a comeback yet, but there are no rules saying you can’t buy a bag of candy and split it with your friends. The days leading to Halloween are always interesting because you get to see all the decorations go up. I like to play the game of choosing which house decor I like the best. Towards the end of the night on Halloween, I just sit on my couch and put on a movie that will scare the absolute living day out of me. Why not? Then not even a month after the night of horrors we have Thanksgiving. Personally, it’s not my favorite holiday of the year for reasons I can’t explain. Maybe it’s because of the not exactly friendly history behind it. But being able to be with my whole family and share a meal together is something I’m thankful for. With my sister leaving for college, Thanksgiving will be the first time I’ll see her. Third Holiday Our third holiday is not actually a holiday, but it’s my birthday. I love my birthday. It’s one of the best days of the year, because it’s an entire day dedicated to me (and all the others who were born on the same day). The day of my birthday is far enough away from December 25th that I still receive birthday and Christmas presents. And being the youngest child helps. The tradition in my family is that when I wake up there are presents at the foot of my bed. I open them with my family and begin the day a happy person. At school everyone says Happy Birthday to you. And then I get to have a party with my family. If it’s on a weekday, later on the weekend there is a party with my friends. And finally, we have my absolute favorite holiday: Christmas. I love Christmas because I have a nice long break from schoolwork, I get to see my sister, and receive presents (obviously). I can’t wait till we buy a Christmas tree, decorate it, blast Christmas music, drink hot chocolate, and feel like a child again. I look forward to this holiday every year because the feelings surrounding it are immaculate. Even if you aren’t religious you still can celebrate. If you take away the religious part, it’s really just being with the ones you love and having a big dinner. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.

articles.text: Mills College in Oakland Oakland’s historic Mills College has announced its merger with Northeastern University in Boston after three months of negotiations, according to an announcement on September 14 by the college trustees. Located in Oakland, the 169-year-old Mills College has been a nationally renowned liberal arts college for women and gender-binary students. It was founded as the Young Ladies Seminary in 1852 and was the first women’s college west of the Rockies. On March 17, Mills College President Elizabeth Hillman announced that the school would no longer enroll first-year students and that the institution would begin to transition its academic programs by creating options and degree pathways for all Mills students. Hillman explained that “the economic burdens of the COVID- 19 pandemic, structural changes across higher education, and budget deficits” led to the decision. Mills had weathered years of financial instability and declining enrollment – in its last year, the prestigious college enrolled just about 900 students, a roughly 30 percent decline since 2015. Faculty, trustees, staff, students and other community stakeholders considered potential structures and programming for a “Mills Institute” following the closure, but the future of a degree-granting college was uncertain. The vote last week answered the long-standing question of how Mills will survive and continue to offer degrees, now as a co-ed program at Northeastern. The college will begin accepting students in July 2022. Northeastern will assume all of Mills’ liabilities and assets, including the college’s 135-acre campus and its extensive art collection. “The benefits that Mills is getting from this agreement are really extraordinary,” Hillman said. “Being able to continue to employ faculty and staff, to remain the anchor institution in East Oakland that we have long been, and to be able to support our students through their degree aspirations – those are all things that we would not have been able to do without this.” Joseph Aoun, President of Northeastern, said that Mills’ campus will become a West Coast anchor for the university’s global operations. “The beautiful Mills campus will become a flagship of Northeastern’s global network, and serve as a premier platform for our signature experiential education and use-inspired research programs. In the coming years, thousands of students and faculty will learn, teach, live, and make breakthrough discoveries on the Mills campus,” he said in a statement. Northeastern is also moving forward with the creation of the Mills Institute, which will be “dedicated to advancing women’s leadership and empowering BIPOC and first-generation students,” Aoun said. Northeastern will “honor and abide by the terms of tenure” for Mills faculty, Hillman said, and will offer tenure-track and adjunct faculty members opportunities for employment. She added that the college will not lay off any staff members. Northeastern University will provide additional details about how the merge effects employees in the coming weeks. Hillman said she will remain president through the transition. Board of Trustees Chair Katie Sanborn said the Board sees the merger as a positive step forward that “will enable the legacy of Mills to endure.” “Northeastern has consistently demonstrated that it respects and values the vital contributions that Mills offers, voicing strong support for integrating the powerful mission of Mills through the Northeastern network,” she said. Mills College students who are scheduled to graduate before June 2022 will receive a degree from Mills, and students who remain at the college through the transition will have their degrees conferred by Mills College at Northeastern University. articles.text: The five Scout troops and Venturing crews in Piedmont are in the midst of a recruiting drive that had been delayed due to COVID-19. The Open Houses that normally occur in March are taking place through the month of September. Thus far, interest and turnout has been high due to pent-up demand and the popularity of Scouting. Thirty prospects accompanied by parents attended a recent Open House by Troop 15, and about one-third were girls. Families of 5th-7th graders say they are seeking a safe environment for socialization and self-improvement. Katherine Scoutmaster Glen Tripp welcomes visiting youth and their parents to an Open House hosted by Troop 15. Photos by Nate Woodley A visiting girl views poster boards showing Scout outings. Most Piedmont troops already have girls in their membership. Parents get their questions answered by Troop 15 Scoutmaster Tripp. 11th-grade Scouts present a slide show to visitors. These sisters crafted survival bracelets at the Open House. 11th-grade Patrol Leader Aidan Weiss teaches a visiting 6th grader. Visiting youth join Scouts in their formation. Benson, Piedmont Council Executive, has confirmed that: • all scoutmasters report that Covid vaccinations or 72-hour clear tests are required for participation; • all registered leaders are required to take youth protection training and keep it updated; • regular conversations are held among the five troops to share best practices. Kids say they go into Scouting because they like being outdoors for camping, swimming, kayaking, outdoor cooking, chopping wood, orienteering, and learning skills such as first aid. Soon, they appreciate the team-building skills that come from being a member of a patrol with roughly seven other similarly-aged kids. Later, they take on positions of responsibility. Parents appreciate that Scouting provides a safe place to learn life skills, build self-efficacy, and explore a wide variety of hobbies. “Scouting is a tremendous program,” said Benson. “There is nothing like it for developing the breadth of skills needed to be prepared for all that life throws at us. We’ve seen how important it is for us to gather together and continue learning in real life, and Scouting is a great way to do that.” Families interested in Cub Scouts (for boys and girls in grades K-5), Scouts BSA (for boys and girls in middle and high school), or Venturing (such as the Piedmont Community Service Crew, for High School students), are invited to contact the council office. For more information, contact Kate Benson at piedmontbsa.org, or call the Scout office at 510-547-4493. articles.text: The 21st Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival filled the city with music and laughter on Sunday, September 19, as local artists shared their talent with an excited and appreciative audience. This year the Piedmont High School Jazz Band, the Bob Roden Quintet, the Albany Big Band, and the Jim Fleser Band took the stage to celebrate Piedmont’s commitment to music and jazz innovation. The Piedmont High School Jazz Band, under the baton of music teacher and director Andria Mullan, opened the festival. The band demonstrated what has become a signature sound of tight horns and lyric rhythm as they moved from the groove of Benny Golson’s “The Cool One” to a free form version of Duke’s” C Jam Blues” that highlighted every artist on the stand. The band’s Jazz Trio then took over with several smooth Latin tinged pieces including a lyric rendition of “Corcovado”. The Bob Roden Quintet then took the stage and led the audience through a lilting rhythmic set that stretched from ballads to bebop. The Quintet centers on the interplay between the smooth sound of Bob Roden on trombone and the soaring lyricism of Ron Jackson on alto sax. The band explored some of the back pages of the American songbook. including “Exactly Like You” and “Blackbird”. In addition the band performed several original pieces such as a Hefti-esque “She Who Makes Happy” and a hard bop, “Penguins of Venus”. The Quintet enjoyed the talents of Jaime Dowd on bass and Dave Casini on drums. The Albany Jazz Big Band, a Festival fixture for several years, took the stage and swung the audience through a medley of standards with their signature sweet horn sound. To the delight of jazz lovers, the band often takes slow, complex ballads, such as “I’ve Got the World on a String” and “All The Things You Are ” and invigorates them with an up-tempo beat and tight horn charts. This allows soloists to enjoy improvisational chord changes in the context of irresistible classic melodies. The Jim Fleser Band brought the Festival to a soaring and lyric conclusion. Fronting a tight band of piano, drums and bass, guitarist Fleser led the audience on a spirited journey through the nuances of jazz. Starting with his Piedmont HS Jazz Trio (Jason Machle, Alex Tafapolsky, Will Davies). trademark hollow body Gibson, Fleser played Freddie Hubbard’s “Red Clay” and Miles Davis’ “Flamenco Sketches”. The clever choice of these trumpet classics worked well on jazz guitar. Fleser changed mid-set to a solid body instrument and used it to great effect on such Afro Cuban pieces as “Bella” and “Europa”. The Albany Big Band Jim Fleser Band bright triplets and sharp bends of the solid body reminded the audience of the versatility of the electric guitar as a jazz instrument and its ability to move seamlessly from cool jazz to Latin-tinged salsa. The 21st annual Festival was a wondrous celebration of music and talent in the sunlight of Piedmont Park. After a year of uncertainty, the smiles of the audience and the music in the warm summer air created a magical joy that was inescapable. Bod Roden Quintet

articles.text: Jack Stein is overall winner in a field of 73 runners Led by Jack Stein, Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team won the first league meet of the season at Point Pinole Regional Park in Richmond last Wednesday, September 15. Stein was the overall winner in a field of 73 runners, clocking a time of 15:50. In a meet with eight schools, the PHS boys were first, and the girls’ team placed fourth. Stein said recently that he hopes to win his first league title, and this was a good start in competition with Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, and Berkeley. “I won a lot of league meets last year and it just didn’t come together in the final. That’s a big goal… Getting my mentality right in races is really important, just making sure I can handle a certain amount of discomfort and still being able to push the pace. That’s something I’ve really been working on,” said Stein, who was 30 seconds faster than second-place Jacob Bull of Castro Valley. Sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse placed third in a time of 16:26.3, and Junior Christian Taylor was close behind in fifth with a time of 16:31.5. Rounding out the top five were sophomore Julien Lee in seventh in 16:33.9, and junior Parker Long in ninth, 16:42. The girls were without lead runner Ellie Black, but sophomore Josephine Oesterer continued her strong start of the season with a fourth-place finish in 19:47.87 in a field of 60 athletes. Oesterer made here varsity debut on September 11 at the Lowell Invitational in San Francisco. Sophomore Jamie Schwarz was ninth in 20:10.26, senior Mara Lovric finished 16th in 20:55.91, junior Violet Lemley was 27th in 21:43.1, and senior Molly McWeeny [laced 32nd in 21:49.8. articles.text: Piedmont’s JV team defeats Trojans 21-16 The Highlanders lost to the Castro Valley Trojans 22-12 under the lights at Witter Field on Friday, September 17 for their league opener in the newly created Mission Valley division of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont was able to generate 176 total rushing yards, but was unable to punch the go-ahead score with a couple of opportunities while trailing 16-12 in the second half. It marks the Trojans’ first win of the season at 1-3. “Despite losing, I think we took a step further this week. 16-kids strong, I’m proud that nobody quit. We’re building, I told them to hold their heads high and have so much to be proud of. At the end of the day, we’re 0-2, but I’m really proud of these kids. We’ll keep working to get it right,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Piedmont opened scoring on the third possession of the game after senior Evan McConathy gained a fumble recovery at CV’s own 17 yard line. But after three straight incompletion, Piedmont sat on 4th-and-10 and offensive coordinator Jamar Julien made the aggressive call to go for it. On a pass over the middle, junior Ryan McConathy broke a tackle with about 4 yards before the marker, taking it to the five. The drama wasn’t over. On a third-down touchdown run from the five by quarterback Nico Defazio, a holding call pushed them back to the 15. The next play on 3rd-and-15, Defazio found Evan McConathy unmanned in the end zone for the leaping grab, making it 6-0 after a missed point after try with 7:36 left in the first quarter. However, Piedmont’s lead was short-lived as Castro Valley scored on its ensuing possession by way of a 71-yard screen to their running back Jalen Melancon breaking several tackles on the way. A two-point conversion made it 8-6 Trojans with 6:30 to go in the first. The Highlanders committed a pair of costly penalties on the next series. Lucas Bernales broke a nine-yard run near midfield, but PHS was penalized 15 yards for blocking in the back. After working their way back to 3rd-and-4, a false start made it 3rd-and-9— leading to a punt. Castro Valley scored on its next possession on a 19-yard pass after eating up over four minutes with 11:50 left in the second quarter, making it 16-6. With 5:29 remaining in the half, PHS retained possession after forcing a turnover on downs from its own 37 yard line. Defazio hit a 10-yard designed keeper on first, followed by runs of seven and 14 yards by Mateo Costa to the 6-yard line. Defazio then scored on another designed keeper, breaking two tackles into the end zone at 3:44. The score became 16-12 after missed 2-point conversion. In the third quarter, Castro Valley got to Piedmont’s 15 before Mason Kimball came through with a sack-fumble on a 4th-and-5. PHS retained possession at its own 22. Piedmont drove down to the CV 17-yard line, including a big 32-yard pass to Evan McConathy, Staff Photo Nico Defazio runs for a Piedmont touchdown in the second quarter.

Highlanders fall 22-12 to Castro Valley Piedmont’s JV team defeats Trojans 21-16 By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlanders lost to the Castro Valley Trojans 22-12 under the lights at Witter Field on Friday, September 17 for their league opener in the newly created Mission Valley division of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont was able to generate 176 total rushing yards, but was unable to punch the go-ahead score with a couple of opportunities while trailing 16-12 in the second half. It marks the Trojans’ first win of the season at 1-3. “Despite losing, I think we took a step further this week. 16-kids strong, I’m proud that nobody quit. We’re building, I told them to hold their heads high and have so much to be proud of. At the end of the day, we’re 0-2, but I’m really proud of these kids. We’ll keep working to get it right,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Piedmont opened scoring on the third possession of the game after senior Evan McConathy gained a fumble recovery at CV’s own 17 yard line. But after three straight incompletion, Piedmont sat on 4th-and-10 and offensive coordinator Jamar Julien made the aggressive call to go for it. On a pass over the middle, junior Ryan McConathy broke a tackle with about 4 yards before the marker, taking it to the five. The drama wasn’t over. On a third-down touchdown run from the five by quarterback Nico Defazio, a holding call pushed them back to the 15. The next play on 3rd-and-15, Defazio found Evan McConathy unmanned in the end zone for the leaping grab, making it 6-0 after a missed point after try with 7:36 left in the first quarter. However, Piedmont’s lead was short-lived as Castro Valley scored on its ensuing possession by way of a 71-yard screen to their running back Jalen Melancon breaking several tackles on the way. A two-point conversion made it 8-6 Trojans with 6:30 to go in the first. The Highlanders committed a pair of costly penalties on the next series. Lucas Bernales broke a nine-yard run near midfield, but PHS was penalized 15 yards for blocking in the back. After working their way back to 3rd-and-4, a false start made it 3rd-and-9— leading to a punt. Castro Valley scored on its next possession on a 19-yard pass after eating up over four minutes with 11:50 left in the second quarter, making it 16-6. With 5:29 remaining in the half, PHS retained possession after forcing a turnover on downs from its own 37 yard line. Defazio hit a 10-yard designed keeper on first, followed by runs of seven and 14 yards by Mateo Costa to the 6-yard line. Defazio then scored on another designed keeper, breaking two tackles into the end zone at 3:44. The score became 16-12 after missed 2-point conversion. In the third quarter, Castro Valley got to Piedmont’s 15 before Mason Kimball came through with a sack-fumble on a 4th-and-5. PHS retained possession at its own 22. Piedmont’s JV football team defeated Castro Valley 21-17 at Witter Field on Friday, September 17, to remain undefeated after two games. articles.text: Exhibit of works by 8 female artists on view through Oct. A group exhibition showcasing a selection of artworks by eight female artists from the East Bay will begin at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, October 2, and will be on view Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. through the month of October or by appointment. An artists’ reception will take place on Sunday, October 3, from noon to 2 p.m. The exhibition features the work of Laura Abrams, Deborah Green, Michelle Lewis, Laura McNall, Juliet Mevi, Jacqui Rubenstein, Ariella Seidenberg, and Caskey Weston. Over 50 works will be on display. “We appreciate this opportunity to present a self-curated show from our personal collections,“ said Deborah Green, the artist who initiated the project. Behold, by Laura Abrams, 12 x 12 Sacred Loons, by Michelle Lewis, 16 x 16 “I am proud to be part of this group of so many talented and accomplished women, and we are looking forward to exhibiting a strong body of artwork in this beautiful space. It’s especially meaningful to be emerging with a collective show after months of pandemic isolation. Works on display showcase a wide variety of styles and media. Growing out of an association through the Northern California Women’s Caucus for Art, many of the artists here embrace its activist mission with works that put forward dynamic feminist, environmental, and social justice messages.” Gallery hours are on Saturdays and Sundays through October 17, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. each day. articles.text: Sistine Chapel, by Nam June Paik The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s exhibition of the work of Nam June Paik will be on display through October 3. The exhibition, which opened in May, includes more than 200 works by the experimental artist who bridged art, music, performance, and technology in groundbreaking ways. The Korean-American artist, who died in 2006, worked with a variety of media and is considered to be the founder of the video art medium. He is credited with the first use of Photo by Andria Lo the term “electronic super highway” to describe the future of telecommunications in 1974. His influence is still felt in pop culture, music, and film in the modern day. The exhibition is the firstever West Coast retrospective. It celebrates Paik’s collaborative approach that transcended genres, traditions, and norms, while also highlighting the playful and profoundly radical work for which he was known. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/nam-june-paik-2021/ for more information on the exhibition, and to obtain tickets. TV Garden, by Nam June Paik Photo by Peter Tijhuis

articles.text: Perspective is a very important component of life. Some people go places and always have a good time. Other people go to the most beautiful places on earth and are miserable. A correspondent wrote to me from one of the most extraordinary places on earth. Cabo San Lucas is one of those places. It is one of the dividing lines of the earth, situated at the far end of the Baja Peninsula at the point where the Pacific Ocean and the Sea of Cortez meet. Gibraltar has a similar reputation as do the southern-most points of South America and Africa. My friends had a wonderful time there. Cabo San Lucas was so intriguing that I did a little bit of research on the Internet. Wouldn’t you know it… One of the reviews was negative in the extreme. That intrigued me. I delved even deeper. Forget the negatives. Let me give you the report as seen by the most objective people I know. International travel to Cabo San Lucas is relatively easy because there are nonstop flights. Medical clearance is also relatively easy. All health precautions are observed, and the hotel can even administer the Covid test. There are many resorts in the area ranging in price from cheap and tawdry to super expensive. The Nobu Hotel was selected. It is a self-contained complex combining a hotel, diverse restaurants, and all sorts of resort activities. At the Nobu there is a calm atmosphere, but it doesn’t cater to old fogeys. Dining is upscale. There is an elegant Japanese restaurant, a gourmet style Mexican restaurant, and a high endsteak restaurant. Three people shared a gigantic tomahawk steak priced at $125. It was supposed to feed two people, but three people couldn’t even finish it. That is just one example. Some of the restaurants have a dress code. Men were well dressed wearing a jacket, tie and slacks, and the women dressed in spectacular fashion. I am keeping the best for last. What is the price tag for all this VIP luxury? Keep in mind that everything was planned by a professional event planner who was the third person in the party. If you booked a room for three nights, you got the fourth night for free. The room for three people was $500 per night. How about some local music during summer? Some of the recent events on the lawn at the Piedmont Center for the Arts inspired me to make the following suggestion: Piedmont should have a municipal band or orchestra playing concerts during the summer – on a regular basis. There have been famous municipal bands in other cities. Why not in Piedmont? Think about the joy provided by the municipal bands of San Francisco and Oakland in the summer at outdoor concerts. Why not here? The Oakland Municipal Band plays at Lake Merritt on weekends, as does the San Francisco Municipal Band at the Music Concourse in Golden Gate Park.

articles.text: The Montclair Lions Club and Montclair Village Association are collaborating to bring back the Restaurant Walk to Montclair Village. Next Tuesday evening, September 28, from 6:00 to 8:30 p.m. a total of 14 merchants will open their doors and provide samples of their food and/or drink. Tickets to the event, called Passports, can be purchased online at MontclairVillage.com, El Agavero Restaurant on Mountain Blvd. is always a favorite stop on the Walk. Showcasing an extensive tequila selection alongside their authentic Mexican cuisine, the Oakland restaurant has three generations of family ownership at the helm in advance at The Book Tree on La Salle Avenue, or in front of US Bank, 1998 Mountain Blvd., on the day of the event. The cost is $30, with proceeds going to support local non-profits, schools, and other worthy causes through the Lions Club. The Restaurant Walk also is an effort to bring some muchneeded attention and patronage to the business owners of Montclair. The Montclair Lions Club will continue the tradition of supporting other service organizations and groups looking to raise some funds for their community work. Any organization wishing to sell a minimum of 10 tickets will receive 50% of the ticket proceeds. That’s $15 per ticket sold. For more information contact Leslie Masler with the Lions Club at 510-213-2530. New this year is the Wine and Beer Tasting Pavilion. Purchase a Wine and Beer Tasting package for an additional $25 and receive artisan wine pours from Wachira Wines, P. Harell Wines, R&B Cellars, and Montclair’s Perle Wine Bar and Bistro. Craft beers will be showcased by Taps and Takeout of Montclair. Wine and Beer tasting tickets are only available online and at the event. For advance tickets see MontclairVillage.com. The annual Restaurant Walk has been on pause for two years due to the COVID pandemic. articles.text: Courtesy of Edward Jones It’s been called the “Great Resignation” – the large number of Americans voluntarily leaving their jobs. If you plan to be part of it (ideally with another source of employment lined up), you’ll need to make the financial moves necessary to keep making progress toward your long-term goals. Here’s some background: After a year in which the pandemic caused so many people to lose their jobs, the economy is opening back up, but the “quit rate” – the number of jobs people have voluntarily left – has been breaking records. Some economists say this high quit rate is because people are confident of getting better jobs, with higher pay and more flexibility to work at home, or because they are preparing to start their own business or join the gig economy. If you’re thinking of joining this temporary migration from the workforce, how can you help ensure that you’ll be financially stable and can continue to make progress toward your long-term goals? Your first move is to look clearly at your financial situation. As mentioned above, it’s best to have new employment in hand before you quit your job. Alternatively, perhaps you have a spouse or life partner who earns enough to sustain the two of you, or you’ve built up an emergency fund that gives you a cushion. However, if your short-term income is less than you previously earned or you need to go without a paycheck for a while, could you still pay your bills? If you are strapped for cash, you might be tempted to tap into your 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan. But this move will generally result in taxes and, if you are younger than 59 ½, a 10 percent penalty as well. Because of this, and because your retirement accounts are designed to be a financial resource after you retire, think twice before dipping into these funds if you leave your current employer. If your employer allows it, you can leave your money in the 401(k) so you’ll still be accumulating resources for retirement. You also have the option to roll those funds into an individual retirement account (IRA) or a new employer’s retirement plan. And if you plan to work for yourself as a freelancer, consultant or business owner, you’ll still want to save toward retirement. Possible retirement plans for the self-employed include an “owner-only” 401(k), a SEP-IRA or a SIMPLE IRA, all of which may be relatively easy to establish and offer tax benefits. A financial advisor can help you find a retirement plan that’s appropriate for your needs. Here’s something else to keep in mind – an emergency fund. As mentioned above, if you already have one, you’ll have some breathing room if you’re thinking of leaving your job and might have a temporary gap in income. But as the name suggests, an emergency fund is there to help cover unexpected costs, such as a major home repair, without forcing you to take out a loan, or cash out part of your longer-term investments. So, if you are planning to tap your emergency fund, work to restock it as soon as possible. If you’re participating in the “Great Resignation,” it means you’re feeling positive about your future employment prospects, which is great. But you’ll want to support that optimism with a strong financial foundation. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a Financial Planner at the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue, Suite 201, Piedmont. Tel. (510) 547-4589.

articles.text: A group of members of Walking on Wednesdays pause in front of the historic Wetmore House at the corner of Vista and Bonita Avenue on September 15. In Dick Carter’s absence this week, a couple of volunteers led a very pleasant walk from the Exedra to Bonita, down Park and into Dracena Park on one of Piedmont’s most scenic and peaceful trails. The attached photo shows Wednesday’s walkers, plus three new walkers, in front of the historic Wetmore House at the corner of Vista and Bonita Avenue. It was built in 1878 by Jess Wetmore and his brother, who constructed it without plans. It is Piedmont’s oldest structure and is now registered with and protected by the National Historic Register. The house was the Wetmore family’s summer home, having been built when it was only one of five homes in the area of farmland. The Wetmore family’s main home was on Clay Street in Oakland. The house in Piedmont had only two owners until 2006. After the last Wetmore family member died, the house was purchased in 1942 by Alice Erskine, an art instructor at Mills College, who appreciated the history of the house. It was she who was able to register the house with the National Register, thus saving it from becoming a city parking lot. She raised her three children there and lived in the house until she died in 2006 at age 97. After viewing the Wetmore House, the walkers ventured over to Dracena Avenue and into Dracena Park. They returned on Ricardo, Arroyo, Monticello and back to central Piedmont on Hillside. articles.text: Doris May Jenkins Lefebre was born on December 5, 1925 in Birkenhead, England. She grew up with her parents Walter and Jane Jenkins, and siblings Jean and Walter. Doris worked as a registered nurse and midwife during the Second World War. She came to the United States in 1953 as a traveling nurse and worked in several states before settling in San Francisco. She continued her vocation as a nurse with Kaiser Permanente in Oakland until retirement. Doris married Werner Baerwald Lefebre in 1958 in San Francisco. They lived happily together until his passing in 1997. Their family home for over 50 years was in Piedmont, California. Doris loved and cared for her home, devoting many hours to perfecting her English garden. She was an aficionado of theatre, opera, symphony, and needlepoint. She was well-traveled, an excellent cook, loved hosting events for her friends and family, and enjoyed spoiling her grandchildren. Doris is predeceased by her husband, brother, and sister. She is survived by her two daughters, Jane Lefebre and Adrienne Moser (Lefebre); son-in-law Victor Moser; and grandchildren Amanda and Taylor Burks, Courtney Gurr (Burks) and husband Nicholas Gurr, and Samuel and Sophia Moser. She also leaves behind three nephews who reside in England. She will be dearly missed by all who knew her. Doris Lefebre, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, passed away on September 5. She was 95.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 22, 2021 25 Obituary Doris Lefebre dies September 5 at 95 Doris May Jenkins Lefebre was born on December 5, 1925 in Birkenhead, England. She grew up with her parents Walter and Jane Jenkins, and siblings Jean and Walter. Doris worked as a registered nurse and midwife during the Second World War. She came to the United States in 1953 as a traveling nurse and worked in several states before settling in San Francisco. She continued her vocation as a nurse with Kaiser Permanente in Oakland until retirement. Doris married Werner Baerwald Lefebre in 1958 in San Francisco. They lived happily together until his passing in 1997. Their family home for over 50 years was in Piedmont, California. Doris loved and cared for her home, devoting many hours to perfecting her English garden. She was an aficionado of theatre, opera, symphony, and needlepoint. She was well-traveled, an excellent cook, loved hosting events for her friends and family, and enjoyed spoiling her grandchildren. Doris is predeceased by her husband, brother, and sister. She is survived by her two daughters, Jane Lefebre and Adrienne Moser (Lefebre); son-in-law Victor Moser; and grandchildren Amanda and Taylor Burks, Courtney Gurr (Burks) and husband Nicholas Gurr, and Samuel and Sophia Moser. She also leaves behind three nephews who reside in England. She will be dearly missed by all who knew her. Doris Lefebre, a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years, passed away on September 5. She was 95.
